title: A desert feeds a rainforest.
teaser: An ocean apart. A connection hiding in the wind.
question: What travels from the Sahara to help the Amazon grow?
options: Seeds carried by migrating birds
Nutrients carried in airborne dust
Fresh water in ocean currents
reveal: The smallest travellers leave the biggest impression.

steps.label: LIFT
steps.text: Winds lift fine mineral dust from the Sahara. The Bodélé Depression in Chad, an ancient lake bed, is one important source.

steps.label: CROSS
steps.text: Some of that dust travels across the Atlantic in the atmosphere. Its journey links a dry landscape to a very wet one.

steps.label: REPLENISH
steps.text: Dust settling over the Amazon carries phosphorus, a nutrient plants need. It helps replace nutrients lost through rain and runoff.

takeaway: A rainforest is connected to landscapes far beyond its own borders.
mapNote: Illustrative connection across the Atlantic; not a forecast or an exact dust trajectory.

source.name: NASA · CALIPSO dust research

title: Two islands. One volcanic family.
teaser: A green giant and a coral ring share a deeper story.
question: What connects volcanic Hawaiʻi and low-lying Midway Atoll?
options: They belong to the same hotspot trail
A river once flowed between them
Both were formed by coral alone
reveal: The Pacific carries a trail of former volcanoes.

steps.label: BUILD
steps.text: Magma rising beneath the Pacific Plate builds volcanoes. The island of Hawaiʻi is near the young, active end of the Hawaiian hotspot trail.

steps.label: MOVE
steps.text: As the plate moves, older volcanoes are carried away from the hotspot. Farther along the island chain, Midway records an older stage of this story.

steps.label: TRANSFORM
steps.text: With time, volcanic islands erode and subside. Coral reefs can grow around them, leaving atolls around the remains of old volcanic foundations.

takeaway: An island is a moment in a much longer geological journey.
mapNote: Illustrative link within the Hawaiian chain; not a reconstruction of past plate positions.

source.name: National Park Service · Oceanic hotspots

title: One ocean. Two distant shores.
teaser: What happens off Japan can reach a Californian harbour.
question: How did the 2011 earthquake off Japan affect California?
options: It shifted California’s coastline east
It sent tsunami waves across the Pacific
It changed the direction of the tides
reveal: The ocean connects places that look worlds apart.

steps.label: DISPLACE
steps.text: The March 2011 Tōhoku earthquake abruptly displaced the seafloor and generated a devastating tsunami near Japan.

steps.label: PROPAGATE
steps.text: Tsunami waves spread across the Pacific basin. They transfer energy over enormous distances rather than carrying the same parcel of water across the ocean.

steps.label: ARRIVE
steps.text: The tsunami damaged harbours as far away as Crescent City and Santa Cruz in California. A distant earthquake became a local coastal event.

takeaway: An ocean separates coastlines on a map—and connects them in reality.
mapNote: Illustrative trans-Pacific connection, not wave heights, travel times, or a warning map. Photos show the places, not the 2011 event.

source.name: USGS · The 2011 Japan earthquake and tsunami

title: A butterfly joins three countries.
teaser: A Canadian summer and a Mexican winter share tiny orange travellers.
question: What links southern Canada to the mountain forests of central Mexico?
options: Monarch butterflies migrating south
The same forest stretching uninterrupted
An underground river
reveal: A continent crossed on wings.

steps.label: DEPART
steps.text: In late summer and autumn, eastern migratory monarchs leave breeding areas in Canada and the United States and head toward central Mexico.

steps.label: SHELTER
steps.text: They overwinter in mountain forests, where oyamel fir trees provide shelter. These small wintering areas are connected to a much larger summer range.

steps.label: RETURN
steps.text: The northward journey involves successive generations. The butterflies reaching Canada are not simply the same individuals completing a round trip.

takeaway: A small winter forest can matter to an entire continent.

source.name: Ontario · Monarch migration

mapNote: Illustrative endpoints of eastern monarch migration, not an individual butterfly’s tracked route.

title: A bird follows two summers.
teaser: Greenland and the Southern Ocean meet in one remarkable life.
question: Why do Arctic terns travel between northern breeding grounds and Antarctic waters?
options: They migrate between seasonal feeding regions
They walk across a permanent ice bridge
Their nests float south on icebergs
reveal: Two ends of Earth. One seasonal journey.

steps.label: NEST
steps.text: Arctic terns breed in northern regions, including Greenland and Iceland, during the northern summer.

steps.label: TRAVEL
steps.text: Tracking research has followed birds from these breeding populations to the Southern Ocean, revealing vast migrations with oceanic stopovers.

steps.label: FEED
steps.text: They spend the southern summer in Antarctic waters before heading north again. Their lives connect productive seas in opposite hemispheres.

takeaway: For a migratory bird, the world is a sequence of seasons.

source.name: British Antarctic Survey · Arctic tern tracking

mapNote: Illustrative polar endpoints. Real tern migrations curve through feeding areas and vary between populations.

title: The ocean reaches inland.
teaser: An Idaho stream has a connection to the Pacific you can’t see on its banks.
question: How can nutrients from the sea reach streams in inland Idaho?
options: Saltwater flows uphill every summer
Returning salmon carry them in their bodies
Ocean spray crosses the mountains
reveal: A fish can carry a piece of the ocean home.

steps.label: GROW
steps.text: Salmon that migrate to sea feed and grow in the ocean, accumulating marine-derived nutrients in their bodies.

steps.label: RETURN
steps.text: Adults travel back through river systems to freshwater spawning areas, including streams in Idaho’s Salmon River basin.

steps.label: RECYCLE
steps.text: Their bodies release nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic matter into receiving ecosystems. Researchers have studied how declining salmon returns affect this inland nutrient supply.

takeaway: A river’s food web can depend on life far beyond its watershed.

source.name: American Fisheries Society · Marine-derived nutrients in Idaho

mapNote: Illustrative ocean-to-basin connection; the arc does not trace the Columbia, Snake, or Salmon rivers.

title: A volcano changed a distant summer.
teaser: An Indonesian eruption left its mark on Europe a year later.
question: How did Tambora’s 1815 eruption affect places far beyond Indonesia?
options: Its lava flowed across continents
It permanently stopped Earth’s seasons
Volcanic aerosols contributed to widespread cooling
reveal: The atmosphere carried the consequences.

steps.label: ERUPT
steps.text: Tambora erupted in Indonesia in 1815, sending volcanic gases high into the atmosphere.

steps.label: SCATTER
steps.text: Sulfur-containing gases formed stratospheric sulfate aerosols that reduced incoming sunlight and contributed to cooling far from the volcano.

steps.label: EXPERIENCE
steps.text: Parts of Europe and North America experienced severe cold and disrupted weather in 1816, remembered as the Year Without a Summer. Effects differed from place to place.

takeaway: An eruption’s reach can extend far beyond the land it covers.

source.name: UCAR · Mount Tambora and the Year Without a Summer

mapNote: Illustrative climate connection, not an ash trajectory. Modern photographs do not show the 1815 eruption or 1816 weather.

title: A morning ritual crossed the Red Sea.
teaser: A forest plant and terraced hills helped shape a familiar cup.
question: Which plant connects Ethiopia’s natural heritage with Yemen’s cultivation history?
options: Cacao
Arabica coffee
Tea
reveal: The name on the bag holds a longer story.

steps.label: ORIGIN
steps.text: Arabica coffee grows wild in northeastern Africa, including Ethiopia. Its botanical origins lie across the Red Sea from Arabia.

steps.label: CULTIVATE
steps.text: Yemen played an important early role in coffee cultivation and use. A crop’s cultivated history can begin somewhere different from its native range.

steps.label: CONNECT
steps.text: These African origins and Arabian cultivation traditions form part of coffee’s wider human story. The species name Arabica alone does not tell the whole journey.

takeaway: An everyday drink can connect botany, landscapes, and human movement.

source.name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Coffea arabica

mapNote: Illustrative regional connection, not a documented shipment route or exact first cultivation site. Photos show the wider landscapes.

title: An Irish staple has Andean roots.
teaser: A familiar food connects green fields with South American highlands.
question: Where does the potato’s domestication story begin?
options: In the Andes of South America
On the coast of Ireland
In the Sahara
reveal: A food’s familiar home may not be its first.

steps.label: DOMESTICATE
steps.text: The cultivated potato has deep roots in the Andes. Kew identifies the Lake Titicaca region of Peru and Bolivia as a probable early domestication area.

steps.label: TRAVEL
steps.text: People carried the crop beyond South America. Its spread eventually made it a familiar food in Europe, including Ireland.

steps.label: RECOGNIZE
steps.text: Andean potato diversity and European potato dishes belong to the same wider story of cultivation and exchange. A local food tradition can have a distant botanical beginning.

takeaway: The history on a dinner plate can cross an ocean.

source.name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Solanum tuberosum

mapNote: Illustrative origin-to-adoption connection; not a direct voyage from Lake Titicaca to Ireland.

sources.name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Solanum tuberosum
American Phytopathological Society · Potato arrival in Europe

title: Distant rains help a desert river flow.
teaser: The green thread through Egypt begins far beyond the desert.
question: What connects rainy Ethiopian highlands with water used downstream in Egypt?
options: A shared underground ocean
The Blue Nile joining the wider Nile system
Rain falling equally across both regions
reveal: A river carries the weather of another landscape.

steps.label: GATHER
steps.text: The Ethiopian highlands receive substantial rainfall despite surrounding dry regions. Lake Tana and its tributaries form part of this highland water system.

steps.label: JOIN
steps.text: The Blue Nile flows from Lake Tana and ultimately joins the White Nile in Sudan. Monsoon rainfall helps supply the Blue Nile.

steps.label: SUPPORT
steps.text: The combined Nile continues downstream toward Egypt. Communities in dry Sudan and Egypt rely on Nile water for irrigation and other uses, connecting them with distant rainfall.

takeaway: A river links people to weather far upstream.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory · Two Niles Meet

mapNote: Illustrative basin connection. The arc is not the river channel; dams, tributaries, and water management also affect downstream flows.

sources.name: NASA Earth Observatory · Two Niles Meet
NASA · Lake Tana and the Ethiopian Highlands

title: Warmth travels across the Atlantic.
teaser: Florida’s offshore waters belong to a much wider ocean story.
question: What carries ocean heat northward and across the North Atlantic?
options: A warm current system including the Gulf Stream
A solid belt of tropical coral
Tides flowing only from west to east
reveal: An ocean current moves more than water.

steps.label: FLOW
steps.text: Warm water moves through the Florida Straits and northward along the eastern United States in the Gulf Stream.

steps.label: TURN
steps.text: The current turns away from the coast and flows northeastward into the Atlantic, linking with a broader ocean circulation system.

steps.label: INFLUENCE
steps.text: Ocean heat transport helps influence western European climate. It works alongside atmospheric circulation and other factors, rather than determining the climate on its own.

takeaway: A coastline’s climate is part of a larger moving system.

source.name: NOAA · Ocean boundary currents

mapNote: Illustrative heat-transport connection. It is not an exact current path, travel time, or claim that one current alone controls Europe’s climate.

title: A London river reaches into the Atlantic.
teaser: An eel in the Thames belongs to a journey much larger than London.
question: What links European eels in the Thames with the Sargasso Sea?
options: They migrate between European waters and Atlantic breeding grounds
They hatch beneath London bridges
The Thames flows directly into that sea
reveal: A hidden life crosses the open ocean.

steps.label: ARRIVE
steps.text: Young European eels reach European coasts after a larval journey through the Atlantic. Some enter estuaries and rivers such as the Thames.

steps.label: GROW
steps.text: They feed and grow in European waters. Barriers in rivers can interrupt access to the habitats they use during this stage of life.

steps.label: RETURN
steps.text: Mature eels migrate back toward their Sargasso Sea breeding region. Satellite tagging has provided direct evidence of adults reaching that region, while details of spawning remain difficult to observe.

takeaway: An urban river can be one chapter of an oceanic life.

source.name: Zoological Society of London · European eel conservation

mapNote: Illustrative life-cycle link, not the track of a Thames eel. The coastal photograph shows Bermuda in the wider Sargasso Sea region.

title: Fossils remember a connected world.
teaser: India and Antarctica were not always separated by an ocean.
question: Why are related ancient land-plant fossils found on continents now far apart?
options: The plants floated over modern oceans intact
The continents were once joined and later separated
Antarctica has always been next to India
reveal: The clues stayed behind as the continents moved.

steps.label: PRESERVE
steps.text: Fossils of plants such as Glossopteris occur across several southern landmasses, including India and Antarctica.

steps.label: COMPARE
steps.text: Matching fossil distributions helped scientists investigate continental drift. They made more sense when the continents were considered as parts of an earlier connected landmass.

steps.label: SEPARATE
steps.text: Plate tectonics explains how continents change position over geological time. Today’s oceans and coastlines are one stage in that continuing history.

takeaway: A modern map is a snapshot, not Earth’s permanent arrangement.

source.name: USGS · Continental drift evidence

mapNote: Modern locations illustrate a past connection; this is not a reconstruction of Gondwana or a precise plate-motion path.

title: An ocean once hid a land connection.
teaser: Australia and New Guinea share a coastline story that sea level rewrote.
question: What once connected Australia and New Guinea during low sea levels?
options: A railway across the ocean
Exposed land that is now underwater
A permanent bridge of sea ice
reveal: A strait was not always a sea.

steps.label: FREEZE
steps.text: During colder phases of the Pleistocene, more water was stored in ice and global sea levels were lower.

steps.label: CONNECT
steps.text: Exposed land connected Australia with New Guinea. The geography available to plants, animals, and people differed from today’s island map.

steps.label: FLOOD
steps.text: When sea levels rose, low-lying connections were flooded. Present coastlines record only the latest part of that history.

takeaway: The edge of a continent can move without the continent moving.

source.name: Australian Museum · The Pleistocene

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: Two continents once shared a passage.
teaser: Alaska and Siberia were connected by more than a narrow crossing.
question: What exposed a land connection between Asia and North America during ice ages?
options: Lower global sea levels
A modern shipping project
A volcanic island growing overnight
reveal: A lost landscape lies beneath the strait.

steps.label: EXPOSE
steps.text: Ice-age sea levels fell, exposing a broad region between present-day Siberia and Alaska known as Beringia.

steps.label: CROSS
steps.text: The connection offered opportunities for species such as mammoths and bison to move between continents. Different animals had different histories.

steps.label: SUBMERGE
steps.text: Rising seas later flooded the connection. The Bering Strait now separates shores that once belonged to a continuous landscape.

takeaway: A narrow strait can conceal a much wider past.

source.name: National Park Service · Beringian megafauna

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: Britain’s island story has a missing chapter.
teaser: The North Sea covers a landscape that once connected neighbours.
question: What was Doggerland?
options: A mountain range in the Pacific
A medieval floating city
A former landscape now beneath the North Sea
reveal: The sea covers an earlier map.

steps.label: CONNECT
steps.text: Britain’s connections with mainland Europe changed repeatedly as climate and sea level changed.

steps.label: INHABIT
steps.text: Doggerland was a landscape through which people and animals could move. The Natural History Museum describes Neanderthals reaching Britain by this route.

steps.label: REIMAGINE
steps.text: Much of that former landscape now lies beneath the North Sea. Understanding Britain’s past means looking beyond its present coastline.

takeaway: An island’s history can begin before it was an island.

source.name: Natural History Museum · First Britons

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: A mountain becomes a city’s floor.
teaser: Stone from the Apuan region connects geology with Florentine craftsmanship.
question: What connects Apuan mountain rock with Florence Cathedral’s floor?
options: Imported rainforest timber
White marble used among its inlaid stones
Lava pumped directly into the building
reveal: A building can hold several landscapes.

steps.label: SOURCE
steps.text: The cathedral’s marble floor combines stone from multiple places. Its official material list includes Apuan white marble.

steps.label: CRAFT
steps.text: Florentine masters designed geometric patterns using contrasting materials. The floor was developed between the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

steps.label: NOTICE
steps.text: Looking at a historic interior can reveal a network of quarries, transport, workshops, and artistic choices—not just one building.

takeaway: Architecture gives distant stone a new address.

source.name: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore · Marble floor

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: A pattern crossed an ocean.
teaser: Indian cloth and British wardrobes share a complicated trade history.
question: What connected Indian weaving and dyeing centres with European consumers?
options: A single shared river
Identical climates
A large trade in cotton textiles
reveal: Cloth carried craft, taste, and power.

steps.label: MAKE
steps.text: Indian producers created cotton textiles for different markets, including finely worked cloth designed for overseas buyers.

steps.label: TRADE
steps.text: European companies imported large quantities of Indian textiles. The V&A documents Coromandel garments made for export to Europe.

steps.label: CONSIDER
steps.text: This exchange also involved exploitation and changing industrial power. Attractive patterns can carry histories of both skill and inequality.

takeaway: An everyday fabric can hold a global history.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum · Indian textiles

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: An inland city became a crossroads.
teaser: China and Samarkand belonged to a network much larger than one road.
question: Why did inland Samarkand become an important centre of exchange?
options: Its position at intersecting trade routes
Its harbour on the Pacific
Its direct canal to China
reveal: Many roads made a meeting place.

steps.label: LINK
steps.text: Trade routes connected China with Central Asia and regions farther west. They formed a network rather than a single uninterrupted road.

steps.label: MEET
steps.text: Samarkand stood at a crossroads of routes from several regions. UNESCO describes its prosperity and role in silk trade.

steps.label: EXCHANGE
steps.text: Goods travelled alongside artistic ideas, beliefs, and knowledge. A city’s importance can come from the connections it makes possible.

takeaway: A crossroads can shape a city as strongly as a coastline.

source.name: UNESCO · Samarkand, Crossroads of Cultures

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: An orchid travelled with a technique.
teaser: Mexico and Madagascar share a familiar flavour with an unfamiliar botanical story.
question: What helped vanilla cultivation spread beyond its native range?
options: Planting the pods upside down
Hand pollination of its orchid flowers
Growing it only in seawater
reveal: A flavour depends on a flower.

steps.label: ORIGIN
steps.text: Vanilla planifolia grows naturally in tropical parts of the Americas, including Mexico. The familiar pod is the fruit of an orchid.

steps.label: CULTIVATE
steps.text: The plant was introduced elsewhere, including Madagascar. Outside its native range, cultivated flowers are generally hand pollinated.

steps.label: TRANSFORM
steps.text: The harvested fruit must be cured to develop its characteristic aroma. A familiar flavour connects plant biology with patient human work.

takeaway: A small flower can link forests, farms, and kitchens.

source.name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Vanilla

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: Chocolate crossed the Atlantic as a drink.
teaser: An American crop became a European luxury long before familiar chocolate bars.
question: In what form did chocolate first become established among wealthy Europeans?
options: Frozen fruit
A modern wrapped bar
A drink made from cacao
reveal: The bar came after a much older story.

steps.label: VALUE
steps.text: Indigenous peoples in Central and South America valued cacao long before Spanish arrival. Cacao beans also served as currency in some areas.

steps.label: CROSS
steps.text: The Spanish brought chocolate to Europe, where the drink was initially associated with royalty and wealthy consumers.

steps.label: CHANGE
steps.text: Its uses and audiences changed over time. The familiar modern product is one chapter in a much longer American and Atlantic history.

takeaway: A sweet taste can carry a history of cultural exchange.

source.name: Smithsonian · Cacao Beans

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: A rainforest tree reshaped distant plantations.
teaser: Amazonian origins and Southeast Asian cultivation meet in natural rubber.
question: Which Amazonian tree became a major plantation crop in Southeast Asia?
options: The rubber tree, Hevea brasiliensis
The olive tree
The date palm
reveal: A material’s origin is not its only home.

steps.label: ORIGIN
steps.text: Hevea brasiliensis is native to parts of tropical South America. Its latex is the main plant source of natural rubber.

steps.label: GROW
steps.text: The tree was introduced to other tropical regions. Kew describes extensive cultivation in Southeast Asia, including Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia.

steps.label: USE
steps.text: The journey connects the biodiversity of one continent with farming and material production on another. Rubber products carry a botanical story.

takeaway: The materials around us often have distant living roots.

source.name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Hevea brasiliensis

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: A seasonal wind helped schedule a voyage.
teaser: India and the Malay Peninsula were connected by winds that changed direction.
question: What helped sailing merchants plan outward and return voyages across the Indian Ocean?
options: A permanent wind blowing one way
Seasonally reversing monsoon winds
A continuous towing cable
reveal: The atmosphere helped set the timetable.

steps.label: OBSERVE
steps.text: Sailors learned how seasonal wind patterns changed across the Indian Ocean. Sailing conditions depended on the time of year.

steps.label: PLAN
steps.text: UNESCO describes ships travelling from India with one monsoon and returning with the opposing seasonal wind.

steps.label: TRADE
steps.text: Ports near the Straits of Malacca became important meeting points in these wider networks. Geography and knowledge of weather shaped commercial connections.

takeaway: A trading route can depend on knowing when to leave.

source.name: UNESCO · Sailing East to West

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: One Pacific shift. Different kinds of weather.
teaser: Peru and Australia can experience opposite sides of the same climate pattern.
question: How can El Niño influence rainfall on opposite sides of the Pacific?
options: It guarantees identical weather everywhere
It changes the length of the year
It shifts ocean warmth and atmospheric circulation
reveal: A connected ocean does not give every coast the same result.

steps.label: SHIFT
steps.text: El Niño involves changes in tropical Pacific ocean temperatures, winds, and rainfall patterns.

steps.label: RESPOND
steps.text: NOAA describes wetter conditions in parts of Peru and drought tendencies in parts of Australia during many El Niño events.

steps.label: DISTINGUISH
steps.text: These are changing probabilities, not guarantees for every place or event. Local conditions and other climate influences also matter.

takeaway: Distant weather patterns can share a cause without sharing an outcome.

source.name: NOAA Climate.gov · Can We Blame El Niño?

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: A familiar fish arrived in an unfamiliar ocean.
teaser: Indo-Pacific origins and Caribbean reefs meet in an invasion story.
question: Why are lionfish in the Caribbean considered invasive?
options: They occur outside their native range and can affect local ecosystems
All reef fish are invasive
They migrate there annually from Antarctica
reveal: Crossing an ocean can change an ecological relationship.

steps.label: BELONG
steps.text: Lionfish are native to the Indo-Pacific, where they form part of long-established marine ecosystems.

steps.label: ESTABLISH
steps.text: They are now established in western Atlantic and Caribbean waters, well outside that native range.

steps.label: AFFECT
steps.text: Lionfish eat small fish and crustaceans and have few predators in these introduced waters. Their spread raises concerns for native ecosystems.

takeaway: A species’ ecological role depends partly on where it lives.

source.name: NOAA · What is a turkeyfish?

mapNote: Illustrative native-to-introduced range comparison, not a natural migration track or documented individual introduction.

title: A whale connects cold feeding seas with warm winter waters.
teaser: Alaska and Hawaiʻi are chapters in one migratory life.
question: Why do many North Pacific humpback whales travel to Hawaiian waters in winter?
options: To feed on Arctic sea ice
To mate, give birth, and raise young
To cross a freshwater lake
reveal: The right habitat changes with the season.

steps.label: FEED
steps.text: Northern waters, including Alaska and Canada, are important seasonal habitats for many North Pacific humpback whales.

steps.label: MIGRATE
steps.text: In winter, many travel thousands of miles to warmer, shallow waters around Hawaiʻi.

steps.label: BREED
steps.text: NOAA describes mating, birth, and the raising of young in these winter waters. Protecting one part of the journey supports only part of their lives.

takeaway: A whale’s home can be an ocean-scale network.

source.name: NOAA Fisheries · Winter habits in Hawaiʻi

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: A technique travelled farther than a sheet of paper.
teaser: China and Baghdad are linked by the movement of papermaking knowledge.
question: What spread westward from China through Central Asia to centres such as Baghdad?
options: The invention of ocean tides
A single intact ancient library
Papermaking techniques
reveal: Skills can travel through a network of people.

steps.label: DEVELOP
steps.text: Papermaking developed in China, creating a material that could carry writing and images.

steps.label: TRANSMIT
steps.text: Knowledge of the craft spread westward. UNESCO describes its transmission through Samarkand and onward to Baghdad.

steps.label: CONNECT
steps.text: This history links workshops, travellers, and centres of learning. The movement of a useful technique can influence places far beyond its origin.

takeaway: Sometimes the most important cargo is knowledge.

source.name: UNESCO · The Paths of New Beliefs

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: A canal connected more than shipping lanes.
teaser: The Red Sea and Mediterranean gained a new ecological connection.
question: How has the Suez Canal influenced Mediterranean ecosystems?
options: It provides a pathway for some non-native species
It removed all differences between the seas
It stops every organism from crossing
reveal: An engineered connection can become a biological one.

steps.label: OPEN
steps.text: The Suez Canal connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean, creating a passage through a former land barrier.

steps.label: MOVE
steps.text: Marine organisms can use this connection. UNEP identifies the canal as a major pathway for non-native species entering the Mediterranean.

steps.label: CHANGE
steps.text: Species introductions can alter existing ecological relationships. Shipping, aquaculture, and other pathways also contribute to marine introductions.

takeaway: Changing a map can change an ecosystem.

source.name: UNEP · Mediterranean non-indigenous species assessment

mapNote: Illustrative connection between seas; not a tracked species route. Photos show regional coastlines.

title: An Icelandic eruption reached European skies.
teaser: A fissure eruption and a distant haze shared the same source.
question: What carried Laki’s effects far beyond Iceland in 1783–84?
options: A river of lava across the sea
Large sulfur emissions and atmospheric transport
A permanent ash bridge
reveal: Air can connect places without a visible road.

steps.label: ERUPT
steps.text: The Laki fissure eruption lasted for months in 1783–84 and had devastating consequences within Iceland.

steps.label: TRANSPORT
steps.text: It released large quantities of sulfur dioxide. Atmospheric transport spread its effects beyond the eruption area.

steps.label: OBSERVE
steps.text: The Met Office describes a sulfurous haze lasting for months across large parts of Europe. Volcanic hazards can extend far beyond nearby lava fields.

takeaway: A distant sky can hold evidence of another landscape’s upheaval.

source.name: Met Office · Volcanic activity in Iceland

mapNote: Illustrative atmospheric connection, not a plume reconstruction. Modern photos do not show the 1783 haze.

title: An Italian favourite has American roots.
teaser: The tomato’s modern culinary home is only part of its story.
question: Where do the tomato’s botanical roots lie?
options: In the European Alps
In the Arctic
In South America
reveal: A recipe can hide an ocean crossing.

steps.label: ORIGIN
steps.text: Tomatoes trace their roots to South America. Kew identifies Peru in the plant’s native-range account.

steps.label: TRAVEL
steps.text: Spanish colonists introduced tomatoes to Europe in the sixteenth century. Acceptance and use changed over time.

steps.label: ADOPT
steps.text: Tomatoes later became central to many European recipes, including Italian sauces. A familiar cuisine can incorporate plants with very distant origins.

takeaway: Culinary identity can grow from exchange.

source.name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Tomato

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: Two shores share a volcanic signature.
teaser: Northern Ireland and a Scottish island display the same striking stone geometry.
question: Why do the Giant’s Causeway and Staffa have similar basalt columns?
options: People carved matching stepping stones
They share related volcanic origins and cooling processes
Ocean waves stacked identical blocks
reveal: Lava cooled into a pattern across two landscapes.

steps.label: ERUPT
steps.text: Ancient volcanic episodes produced basalt across this region. BGS links Staffa’s columnar rocks with the episodes behind the Giant’s Causeway.

steps.label: COOL
steps.text: As thick lava cools and contracts, cracks can develop into regular networks, dividing the rock into columns.

steps.label: COMPARE
steps.text: The two coastlines preserve related geological stories. Their resemblance offers evidence of shared physical processes rather than human construction.

takeaway: A pattern in stone can reveal a relationship across the sea.

source.name: British Geological Survey · Giant’s Causeway

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: Two deserts meet cold ocean water.
teaser: The Namib and Atacama show how a dry coast can still receive fog.
question: What helps explain the fog associated with these coastal deserts?
options: Warm rivers from tropical forests
Permanent sheets of sea ice
Moist air interacting with cold coastal waters
reveal: Similar physics can shape landscapes an ocean apart.

steps.label: UPWELL
steps.text: Cold ocean waters occur beside both desert coasts. Offshore winds and ocean circulation help bring deeper water toward the surface.

steps.label: CONDENSE
steps.text: Moist air cooled near the ocean surface can form fog even where rainfall is scarce.

steps.label: DISTINGUISH
steps.text: These deserts have different histories and additional climate influences. The connection is a shared coastal process, not a single current joining them.

takeaway: Rainfall is not the only way moisture reaches a desert.

source.name: NASA My NASA Data · Ocean circulation stories

mapNote: Comparison of two coastal environments, not a transport route between them. Photos show the wider desert regions.

title: A desert preserves a vanished shoreline.
teaser: Modern Lake Chad and distant desert ridges belong to one changing water story.
question: Why are ancient beach ridges found far from modern Lake Chad?
options: A much larger lake once occupied the region
Modern oceans flood the Sahara every year
The ridges were built by ships
reveal: The shore moved, but the evidence remained.

steps.label: EXPAND
steps.text: During a wetter period, Lake Mega Chad occupied a vastly larger area than the modern lake.

steps.label: SHAPE
steps.text: Waves and currents formed shore features including beach ridges and sand spits.

steps.label: REVEAL
steps.text: NASA satellite and elevation observations reveal those former shorelines in today’s dry landscape, hundreds of kilometres from modern waters.

takeaway: A dry landscape can preserve the shape of past water.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory · Remnants of an Ancient Lake

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: A narrow crossing changed ocean travel.
teaser: Two coasts of Panama connect ships with routes far beyond Central America.
question: What does the Panama Canal connect for ocean-going ships?
options: The Arctic and Southern oceans
The Atlantic and Pacific oceans
The Mediterranean and Red seas
reveal: A short crossing reshaped long journeys.

steps.label: SEPARATE
steps.text: The Isthmus of Panama divides Atlantic and Pacific waters across a comparatively narrow strip of land.

steps.label: CONNECT
steps.text: The canal provides a navigable crossing between the oceans, changing the distances and routes available to ships.

steps.label: NETWORK
steps.text: Its importance extends to ports worldwide. A local piece of infrastructure can become part of a global trading network.

takeaway: A small place on a map can change the shape of a world journey.

source.name: Panama Canal Authority · Connectivity

mapNote: Illustrative coast-to-coast link, not the canal’s exact channel, lock layout, or a recommended shipping route.

title: A lowland river remembers alpine snow.
teaser: The Rhine links Swiss mountain waters with the Netherlands.
question: How do alpine snow and ice influence the Rhine?
options: They freeze all Dutch rivers permanently
They reach the delta only as icebergs
Their seasonal melt contributes to river flow
reveal: A river carries more than the weather beside its banks.

steps.label: STORE
steps.text: Snowfields and glaciers store some precipitation in the Alps, delaying its release as flowing water.

steps.label: RELEASE
steps.text: Seasonal melting contributes to the Rhine’s flow. The river’s tributaries and rainfall patterns add other influences downstream.

steps.label: CONNECT
steps.text: The Rhine system reaches the Netherlands, linking lowland water management with conditions across its upstream basin.

takeaway: Downstream water has an upstream calendar.

source.name: International Commission for the Protection of the Rhine · Runoff

mapNote: Illustrative river-basin connection; the arc does not follow the Rhine’s channel or individual distributaries.

title: A mountain range helps build a delta.
teaser: Himalayan erosion and Bangladesh’s lowlands are connected by moving sediment.
question: What do rivers carry from Himalayan highlands toward the delta?
options: Sediment eroded from the land
Coral reefs growing on mountain peaks
Ocean salt moving uphill
reveal: What leaves a mountain can become part of a lowland.

steps.label: ERODE
steps.text: Rivers and streams remove material from Himalayan landscapes, including rapidly eroding parts of the eastern range.

steps.label: TRANSPORT
steps.text: Sediment-rich rivers such as the Brahmaputra move that material through valleys and floodplains.

steps.label: DEPOSIT
steps.text: Sediment accumulates downstream, including in the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta. Deposition, erosion, flooding, and subsidence continue to reshape the land.

takeaway: Mountains and deltas are stages in the same material journey.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory · The Braided Brahmaputra

mapNote: Illustrative mountain-to-delta connection; not a traced river channel. The mountain photograph represents the wider Himalayan range.

title: A mountain wall changes the story of moisture.
teaser: The Amazon’s humid interior and the Andes reveal what happens when winds meet mountains.
question: What happens when moisture-bearing air meets the Andes?
options: The mountains erase every cloud
The terrain influences rainfall and rain shadows
Rain falls equally on every slope
reveal: A mountain can separate very different climates.

steps.label: CARRY
steps.text: Winds transport moisture from the South American interior toward the eastern slopes of the Andes.

steps.label: RISE
steps.text: Mountain topography influences where air rises and precipitation falls, contributing to wetter eastern conditions.

steps.label: CONTRAST
steps.text: NASA observations show humid rainforest and much drier landscapes toward the Pacific side. Rain shadows help explain part of this contrast.

takeaway: Neighbouring landscapes can differ because of the air between them.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory · Looking Down on the Andes

mapNote: Illustrative atmospheric and terrain connection, not a specific air parcel’s trajectory. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: An inland lake belongs to an ocean network.
teaser: The Great Lakes connect North America’s interior with Atlantic navigation.
question: What links Great Lakes shipping with the Atlantic Ocean?
options: A canal through the Rocky Mountains
A seasonal sea-ice road
The Great Lakes–St. Lawrence navigation system
reveal: A coastline is not the only doorway to the sea.

steps.label: JOIN
steps.text: The Great Lakes and St. Lawrence form a connected water system reaching toward the Atlantic.

steps.label: NAVIGATE
steps.text: Locks and other infrastructure help ships move through changes in water level along the navigation system.

steps.label: TRADE
steps.text: The route connects inland producers and ports with wider markets. Its economic geography extends well beyond an ocean shoreline.

takeaway: An inland port can have an ocean-scale reach.

source.name: U.S. Seaway Development Corporation · The Seaway System

mapNote: Illustrative inland-to-estuary connection; not a navigation chart or a trace of the full lock system.

title: Two neighbouring seas do not taste the same.
teaser: The North Sea and Baltic show how gateways and rivers affect salinity.
question: Why is much of the Baltic Sea brackish rather than as salty as the open ocean?
options: Freshwater inflow mixes with limited seawater exchange
Its water is made entirely of melted ice
Salt cannot pass through straits
reveal: The connection matters—and so does its size.

steps.label: EXCHANGE
steps.text: Marine water enters the Baltic from the North Sea through its restricted entrance region.

steps.label: DILUTE
steps.text: Numerous rivers supply freshwater. Together these flows produce a salinity gradient across the Baltic.

steps.label: INFLUENCE
steps.text: Water exchange is comparatively slow. These conditions help shape the sea’s habitats and the organisms able to live there.

takeaway: A sea’s character depends on what enters and what can leave.

source.name: HELCOM · About the Baltic Sea

mapNote: Illustrative exchange between sea regions; not a current forecast or exact strait-by-strait path.

title: A Japanese record helped reveal an American earthquake.
teaser: Written observations and coastal clues met across the Pacific centuries later.
question: Why was Japan’s January 1700 tsunami called an “orphan” tsunami?
options: It happened in a freshwater lake
No nearby parent earthquake had been felt
It had no waves
reveal: Distant records helped scientists connect the clues.

steps.label: RECORD
steps.text: Japanese observers documented flooding and damage in January 1700 without feeling a local earthquake.

steps.label: COMPARE
steps.text: Researchers later compared these accounts with evidence of a major earthquake along the Cascadia coast.

steps.label: CONNECT
steps.text: The combined evidence linked the tsunami with its distant earthquake source, showing the value of records from opposite sides of an ocean.

takeaway: A scientific answer can be assembled from clues held far apart.

source.name: USGS · The Orphan Tsunami of 1700

mapNote: Illustrative historical connection, not a wave forecast. Modern place photographs do not depict the 1700 event.

title: A volcano brought distant observers into one investigation.
teaser: An Indonesian eruption and British records became part of a worldwide scientific effort.
question: How did observers far from Krakatoa help investigate its 1883 eruption?
options: By collecting lava in British rivers
By stopping the eruption remotely
By reporting unusual skies and atmospheric observations
reveal: The connection was written in skies and instruments.

steps.label: ERUPT
steps.text: Krakatoa’s violent 1883 eruption had effects well beyond Indonesia, including atmospheric disturbances and unusual visual phenomena.

steps.label: REPORT
steps.text: The Royal Society’s investigation gathered reports about pressure, sound, sea level, dust, and extraordinary light and colour.

steps.label: COMPARE
steps.text: British sunset descriptions joined observations from other places. Combining many records helped scientists investigate a global event.

takeaway: A distant observer can contribute to understanding a local catastrophe.

source.name: Royal Society · Crowdsourcing Krakatoa

mapNote: Illustrative observation network link, not an ash plume or sound-propagation path. Photos show modern places.

title: A mining landscape had a second life overseas.
teaser: Cornwall and South Australia share technology, skills, and family histories.
question: What helped connect Cornish mining communities with Moonta?
options: The movement of mining skills, technology, and people
A river running between the mines
Identical names chosen by chance
reveal: People carried a working landscape across the world.

steps.label: INNOVATE
steps.text: Cornwall developed influential mining technology and specialist skills during its period of industrial expansion.

steps.label: TRANSFER
steps.text: Moonta and Burra became important sites for the transfer of Cornish mining and Welsh smelting technology to Australia.

steps.label: REMEMBER
steps.text: Mine remains and community histories preserve these links. Industrial heritage is also a story of migration and knowledge.

takeaway: A landscape can have relatives through the people who worked it.

source.name: National Trust of Australia · Moonta Mines heritage

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: A Chinese workshop answered a Portuguese order.
teaser: Porcelain connected distant makers with unfamiliar symbols and new customers.
question: What shows that Chinese porcelain was being made for Portuguese customers?
options: All porcelain was manufactured in Lisbon
Export pieces decorated with Portuguese royal arms
A natural porcelain reef between the countries
reveal: An object can preserve a conversation across cultures.

steps.label: TRADE
steps.text: Portuguese maritime routes helped Chinese porcelain reach European customers in greater quantities during the early sixteenth century.

steps.label: DESIGN
steps.text: Chinese potters produced objects specifically for export. The Metropolitan Museum describes an early ewer with Portugal’s royal arms.

steps.label: INTERPRET
steps.text: On that object, the arms were painted upside down. Even a small design detail can reveal the challenges of working across unfamiliar visual traditions.

takeaway: Trade can move symbols as well as objects.

source.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art · Chinese Export Porcelain

mapNote: Illustrative production-region-to-customer connection, not a documented shipment from a specific kiln. Photos show wider regions.

title: A Javanese monument holds connections across the sea.
teaser: Borobudur’s art combines a local setting with wider Buddhist artistic traditions.
question: What connection does UNESCO identify in Borobudur’s artistic style?
options: It was carved from Antarctic ice
It copies modern European factories
Influences from Indian Buddhist artistic traditions
reveal: Ideas can travel and become something locally distinctive.

steps.label: SHARE
steps.text: Buddhist ideas and artistic traditions circulated across Asia through wider cultural connections.

steps.label: CREATE
steps.text: Borobudur developed as a major Javanese monument. Its art includes influences associated with Indian Gupta and post-Gupta styles.

steps.label: DISTINGUISH
steps.text: Recognizing influence does not make it a simple copy. A monument can express both local creativity and connections with a wider artistic world.

takeaway: Cultural connections can generate new forms of beauty.

source.name: UNESCO / ICOMOS · Borobudur evaluation

mapNote: Illustrative cultural connection, not proof of a direct route from the photographed Indian monument to Borobudur.

title: A Roman square can hold an Egyptian past.
teaser: Monuments moved across the Mediterranean along with imperial power.
question: Why are ancient Egyptian obelisks found in Rome?
options: Roman rulers transported Egyptian monuments to the city
They grew naturally from Roman soil
All Egyptian monuments were built in Italy
reveal: A monument’s current address may hide an earlier one.

steps.label: CONQUER
steps.text: After Rome conquered Egypt, the region became an important province of the Roman Empire.

steps.label: TRANSPORT
steps.text: Works and monuments, including obelisks, were taken to Rome to decorate places and celebrate imperial conquest.

steps.label: REINTERPRET
steps.text: Egyptian culture also influenced Roman artistic production. The connection involves both transported objects and newly created interpretations.

takeaway: An urban landmark can carry the history of another country.

source.name: Vatican Museums · Egypt and Rome

mapNote: Illustrative Egypt–Rome connection; not the documented transport route of one specific obelisk.

title: A familiar Indian heat has American roots.
teaser: Chillies connect kitchens across an ocean and centuries of exchange.
question: What is the broader origin story of Capsicum chillies used in Indian cooking?
options: They originated in Himalayan glaciers
They came from the Americas and spread through trade
They were always native to every tropical country
reveal: A cuisine can adopt a distant plant and make it its own.

steps.label: ORIGIN
steps.text: Capsicum peppers have American origins. Their species include the familiar cultivated chilli pepper Capsicum annuum.

steps.label: SPREAD
steps.text: Seeds reached Europe and were then planted widely through Portuguese connections in Africa and Asia, including India.

steps.label: ADOPT
steps.text: Regional cooks incorporated chillies in distinctive ways. A plant’s native range and its later culinary importance need not match.

takeaway: A local flavour can preserve a global journey.

source.name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Capsicum annuum

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: A North American flower found distant fields.
teaser: The sunflower connects its native continent with cultivation in Ukraine.
question: How can a plant strongly associated with Ukraine also have North American origins?
options: Its seeds can only grow in one country
Ukraine and North America share a land border
Plants can be introduced and cultivated far beyond their native range
reveal: A familiar field can contain a faraway botanical history.

steps.label: ORIGIN
steps.text: The common sunflower, Helianthus annuus, is native to North America.

steps.label: INTRODUCE
steps.text: People carried the species beyond its original range. Kew records Ukraine among the places where it has been introduced.

steps.label: CULTIVATE
steps.text: Its wider cultivation shows how human choices can reshape a plant’s geographical story. A strong modern association does not establish native origin.

takeaway: A plant can become part of a place without beginning there.

source.name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Sunflower

mapNote: Illustrative native-to-introduced range comparison. Landscape photos show the wider regions, not verified sunflower fields.

title: A grain connects Mexico with African tables.
teaser: Maize shows how a crop can travel and become important in new food traditions.
question: What connects maize grown in Kenya with Mexico?
options: The crop’s Mesoamerican origins and later worldwide spread
An underground grain pipeline
Its dependence on identical seasons in both countries
reveal: A shared crop can link very different landscapes.

steps.label: DOMESTICATE
steps.text: Maize is associated with domestication in Mesoamerica, including Mexico. It developed through human cultivation rather than appearing as today’s crop everywhere.

steps.label: SPREAD
steps.text: The crop spread beyond the Americas and became widely cultivated in other warm regions, including parts of Africa.

steps.label: ADAPT
steps.text: Different communities developed their own farming and food traditions around it. Shared botanical origins can coexist with distinct local identities.

takeaway: A staple food can have both a local culture and a distant beginning.

source.name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew · Zea mays

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: A British ritual began with an imported drink.
teaser: Tea links East Asian cultivation with changing habits in Britain.
question: How did tea become part of British life?
options: It arrived naturally in North Sea currents
It was imported through maritime trade and later adopted widely
It was first cultivated beneath London streets
reveal: A daily habit can begin as a distant luxury.

steps.label: TRADE
steps.text: European merchants encountered tea through Asian maritime trade. The V&A describes imports from China and Japan.

steps.label: VALUE
steps.text: Its high cost initially made tea a luxury. Trade and imperial expansion shaped who supplied it and who could afford it.

steps.label: ADOPT
steps.text: Drinking habits and teapot designs changed as tea became established in Britain. A familiar ritual carries a history of exchange and unequal power.

takeaway: What feels traditional can be the result of long-distance connections.

source.name: Victoria and Albert Museum · Teapot design through time

mapNote: Illustrative connection between modern places, not an exact historic route. Photographs show the wider regions.

title: A British summer bird has a southern chapter.
teaser: Swallows connect familiar countryside with habitats far beyond Europe.
question: Where do many swallows seen breeding in Britain travel for the northern winter?
options: They remain in Britain throughout winter
They migrate to Arctic breeding grounds
South through Africa, including South Africa
reveal: The bird above a field belongs to a much larger journey.

steps.label: BREED
steps.text: Swallows visit Britain during the warmer part of the year, feeding on flying insects and breeding in suitable habitats.

steps.label: DEPART
steps.text: As autumn approaches, they gather before migrating south through Europe and Africa.

steps.label: RETURN
steps.text: The RSPB describes British swallows reaching South Africa before returning north in spring. Their needs extend across many landscapes and borders.

takeaway: A summer visitor depends on places you may never see.

source.name: RSPB · Swallow

mapNote: Illustrative seasonal endpoints, not the tracked route of one bird. Populations and journeys vary.
